items.label: fc03-incident-note
items.front: What six things does the debugging laboratory require in the closing incident note?
items.back: Symptom, hypothesis rejected, minimal failing input, intended rule, verified repair, and missing evidence - written so another learner can reproduce the failure from the input alone, without your editor state.

items.label: fc01-evidence-lab
items.front: unionboot: how do you run the isolated merge-boundaries evidence lab, and what does it deliberately not do?
items.back: `node --test advanced-practice/merge-boundaries.test.cjs` from the repo root. It imports the real 3439 reference and proves boundary behavior - without grading learner starters, editing starters, writing reports, or downloading packages.

items.label: fc02-proto-fixture
items.front: Building a test record with an own '__proto__' key: why is an object literal the wrong tool?
items.back: A literal's __proto__ definition has special semantics (it targets the prototype), so it may not create the own data property you intended. Parse JSON instead - '{"__proto__":"data"}' creates an ordinary own key - and inspect Object.hasOwn on the fixture before drawing conclusions.

items.prompt: A teammate changes the conflict branch to keep base 'to avoid losing data'. Why does D3 reject this repair even though it feels safer?

choices.text: Keeping base is slower because it forces a third property lookup per key
The change makes conflicts unsorted, breaking the lexicographic guarantee
Base may itself be missing the key, so keeping base can throw at runtime
It silently rewrites the published local-wins policy - product policy belongs in the contract, and the locally-deleted-key assertion exists to catch exactly this improvisation

items.explanation: The lab's lesson: code should not improvise a different policy during an exceptional-looking case. The contract says conflicts keep local, including local deletions.

items.prompt: The debugging lab's D1 hypothesis claims nullish coalescing discards empty strings. What do `'' ?? 'fallback'` and `'' || 'fallback'` each evaluate to?

choices.text: 'fallback' and 'fallback' - both operators treat the empty string as missing
'' and 'fallback' respectively - ?? falls back only for null or undefined, while || falls back for every falsy value
'' and '' - both operators keep any string operand, empty or not
'fallback' and '' - nullish coalescing is the stricter of the two about emptiness

items.prompt: Why does the 3439 reference represent deletion with a fresh Symbol instead of a fallback string like 'absent'?

choices.text: Strings are compared by locale rules, which makes sentinel equality unreliable
Because empty strings are nullish, only a symbol survives the ?? operator
Every string is inside the value domain, so a string sentinel can collide with a legitimately stored value; a unique symbol can never equal any input string
Symbols serialize to JSON more compactly than strings do

items.explanation: The guide's fallback-collision case: base holds a value equal to the fallback string, and missing versus unchanged become indistinguishable. The guide also debunks 'empty strings are nullish' explicitly - they are not.

items.prompt: In capstone 3439, base, local and remote all hold different states for the same key. What does the merge produce for it?

choices.text: The key is recorded in conflicts and local's state wins - even when local's change is a deletion, which removes the key from value while keeping its name in conflicts
Base's value is restored, since neither edit can be trusted over the ancestor
Remote wins because remote edits are assumed newer, and the key is flagged
The key is dropped from both value and conflicts until a human resolves it

items.explanation: The prompt's final rule: otherwise record a conflict and keep local (including local deletion). A conflicted local deletion is the subtle case the worked trace drills.

items.prompt: The contract requires conflicts to be lexicographically sorted. How does the reference satisfy this without ever sorting the conflicts array?

choices.text: The union of own keys is sorted once and visited in that order, so conflict names are pushed already in lexicographic order
conflicts is a Set, which iterates its members in sorted order
Object.fromEntries sorts its entries as a side effect of defining them
The verifier sorts the array before comparing, so order never matters

choices: The union of own keys is sorted once and visited in that order, so conflict names are pushed already in lexicographic order
conflicts is a Set, which iterates its members in sorted order
Object.fromEntries sorts its entries as a side effect of defining them

items.explanation: `for (const key of [...allKeys].sort())` is the single O(k log k) step; everything downstream inherits the order - a design worth stealing for 'sorted output' requirements.

items.prompt: Why does the reference assemble its result with Object.fromEntries instead of assigning result[key] = value in the loop?

choices.text: fromEntries deduplicates repeated keys, which the sorted union cannot guarantee
fromEntries is faster because it preallocates the object's hidden class

fromEntries defines each pair as an own data property, so a '__proto__' key becomes ordinary data; direct assignment would invoke the inherited __proto__ setter, and a string value would simply be ignored
Direct assignment would replace the result's prototype with the string value

items.prompt: A record's side of the merge is read with plain `record[key]`. What misclassification does D2 demonstrate?

choices.text: Numeric keys are coerced to strings, so 1 and '1' collide in the union
Getters run twice, so side effects double when the key is read for both sides
undefined own values disappear, because bracket lookup skips undefined entries
An inherited property of the same name reads as present, so a side that does not own the key is treated as if it had a value - only an Object.hasOwn check asks about ownership

choices: Numeric keys are coerced to strings, so 1 and '1' collide in the union

undefined own values disappear, because bracket lookup skips undefined entries
An inherited property of the same name reads as present, so a side that does not own the key is treated as if it had a value - only an Object.hasOwn check asks about ownership

items.explanation: The reference's read() helper returns the missing sentinel unless Object.hasOwn(record, key) - lookup answers 'what value is visible', hasOwn answers 'does this record own the key'.

items.prompt: Worked trace: base {title:'draft', note:'absent', empty:'x'}, local {title:'edited', empty:''}, remote {title:'draft', note:'revised', empty:''}. What comes out?

choices.text: value = {empty:'', title:'edited'} and conflicts = ['note'] - note is a conflicted local deletion
value = {empty:'x', title:'edited'} and conflicts = ['empty'] - the editors disagree with base about empty
value = {title:'edited'} and conflicts = ['note','empty'] - deletions win both contested keys
value = {empty:'', note:'revised', title:'edited'} and conflicts = [] - each side changed different keys

value = {empty:'x', title:'edited'} and conflicts = ['empty'] - the editors disagree with base about empty
value = {title:'edited'} and conflicts = ['note','empty'] - deletions win both contested keys

items.explanation: empty: both editors agree on '' (keep it). title: remote still matches base, local's edit wins. note: local deleted, remote revised - both moved, conflict, local deletion wins.
